To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the density dependence of yield, plant length and reproductive output of two subtidal marine species is the opposite of what is expected for terrestrial plants.

(1) for two subtidal marine species of algae, total yield, plant length and plant weight were all greater at higher densities; (2) the 3/ 2 thinning law did not hold for these two species; and (3) the effects of density on marine plants may be due to differences in herbivory by arthropods in marine and terrestrial floras.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of density on monotypic stands of marine algae, and the possible causes of these effects.
the effect of density on the growth and reproduction of marine algae, in the absence of grazing.

the following: (1) the effects of density on the biomass, length and weight distributions of plants in monospecifc stands; (2) the relationship of these characters to time and to each other; (3) the effects of plant size on mortality.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of density on plant stands are dependent on the system studied.
the effects of density on plants are not universal.
terrestrial plants are negatively affected by crowding and competition whereas subtidal marine plants are positively affected by density.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
marine algae are more like trees than like terrestrial plants.
the density effects in terrestrial plants are due to the effects of herbivores, while in marine plants, the effects of density are not due to herbivores.
the 3/ 2 thinning law is not applicable to algae.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of density on marine algae are the reverse of what is expected from work on terrestrial plants.
the effects of plant–plant interactions on the growth and survival of individuals in a stand are not universal, but depend on the particular species and environment.
the density effects observed in terrestrial plants do not necessarily hold in marine systems.
